title: Message persistence and ordering
description: Project: Message persistence and ordering. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Messages in a collaborative platform are not transient; they are the system of record. Persistence guarantees that messages survive server restarts, and ordering guarantees that users read them in the sequence the speakers intended. Achieving both at scale requires choosing the right storage engine, write path, and synchronization protocol.

items: Persist every message to durable storage before acknowledging to the sender
Use a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation to enforce total ordering
Separate the write path from the broadcast path to avoid blocking message delivery on persistence
Choose a database optimized for append-heavy workloads: PostgreSQL with integer sequences, Cassandra, or ScyllaDB
Handle clock skew by using server-assigned timestamps, not client clocks
Design pagination by sequence number or timestamp to support infinite scroll without offset-based queries
Implement tombstoning for deletions and edits so history remains consistent across devices

terms.definition: A storage pattern where new records are only ever added and never modified in place, preserving a complete history.
A monotonically increasing integer assigned by the server to each message in a conversation, providing a total order.
A marker indicating that a message has been deleted or redacted, without removing the original record.
A unique identifier generated by the client for each message, allowing the server to safely process retries without creating duplicates.
An opaque value representing a position in a result set, used to fetch the next page without skipping or repeating rows.

data.text: Users expect message history to be permanent and ordered. A platform that loses messages after a server restart or shows them out of sequence will not earn user trust. Ordering bugs are especially pernicious because they are intermittent and depend on timing; they often surface only under load or after failover.

data.title: Persist before broadcast
data.text: Always write the message to the database and obtain a sequence number before broadcasting it to other users. If you broadcast first and the server crashes before persisting, the message vanishes for everyone except the sender. Persist-then-broadcast guarantees durability.

items: Client sends message with a client-generated idempotency key and payload
Server validates auth and subscription to the conversation
Server assigns a server timestamp and a sequence number using an atomic counter per conversation
Server writes the message to the database in a single transaction
Server publishes the message to the message bus for real-time delivery
Server returns the persisted message with its sequence number to the sender
Other recipients receive the message via WebSocket and append it to their local cache

data.title: Design a message schema and write path
data.description: Design the database schema and API write path for a message service that must support ten thousand messages per second with exactly-once delivery semantics.
steps: Create a messages table with idempotencyKey, conversationId, senderId, payload, serverTimestamp, sequenceNumber, and tombstone flag
Design a sequences table to generate monotonic sequence numbers per conversation without gaps
Write the API endpoint that receives a message, validates it, assigns a sequence number, and persists it
Add a unique index on idempotencyKey per conversation to reject duplicates
Design the pagination query using sequenceNumber as a cursor
Write a tombstone update that marks a message as deleted without removing the row
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a schema and write path that guarantees ordering, deduplication, and durable history.

items.question: Should I use a single global sequence or per-conversation sequences?
items.answer: Per-conversation sequences are simpler for ordering within a thread and scale better. Global sequences are useful for a unified activity feed but add contention.

items.question: How do I handle gaps in sequence numbers?
items.answer: Gaps are acceptable and expected. Use sequence numbers only for ordering within a conversation, not for counting or continuity checks. If a gap occurs, the client should request the missing range from the server.

items.question: What if two servers assign the same sequence number?
items.answer: Prevent this by centralizing sequence generation in one service or using atomic database operations. Do not generate sequence numbers in application memory without coordination.

data.title: Summary
points: Persist messages before broadcasting to avoid loss
Use server-assigned sequence numbers for total ordering
Design pagination around sequence numbers, not offset
Handle deletions with tombstones, not physical deletes
data.takeaway: Message persistence is the foundation of trust in a communication platform. Get the write path right and the rest of the system becomes much simpler.
